speakeroldname: Mr. Barry Moore (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF MULTICULTURALISM AND CITIZENSHIP ACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is with a great deal of pleasure that I open third reading debate on Bill C-18. The minister could not be here today due to a long-standing commitment he had in Winnipeg.
We are now in the final phase of deliberations on Bill C-18, an act to establish the Department of Multicultur-alism and Citizenship.
Moving this bill through its final stages in the House and on to the other place follows a strong commitment of the Prime Minister reaffirmed a few weeks ago in Toronto. The Prime Minister did so because he knows this department will help strengthen our sense of being Canadian and promote equality for all in Canada.

Last June the Secretary of State told the legislative committee to which Bill C-18 had been referred that it was nothing more than a housekeeping measure. In short, it is a bill concerning government management and aimed at establishing a new department.
In the debate on this bill we have heard small voices rooted in the past, urging Canadians to look backward, urging Canadians to grind the wheels of social progress to a halt.
We have listened to some hon. members in the Opposition. The government has reviewed the amendments they proposed at committee stage and in the House, amendments that go far beyond the scope of this bill.
As the minister explained in detail at committee hearings on Bill C-18, this legislation is an administrative measure to provide the legal framework for a department. It does not in any way replace the Multicul-turalism Act or the Citizenship Act.
Yet, time and time again, my hon. colleagues have been critical of the bill because it does not include a definition of multiculturalism. Quite frankly, their logic is elusive.
I would direct my hon. colleagues to read the title of the bill. We are not talking about a department of multiculturalism only. Do members of the opposition suggest we be so flippant as to dismiss the citizenship mandate of this department? Why are they only speaking to one side of the department?
None of them over there has even given the slightest thought to the imbalance that will arise if we defend multiculturalism and do not do the same for citizenship. They do not understand that we have given a much broader scope to this institution than just multiculturalism.
Maybe they just were not listening, or maybe they were only listening to certain overly vocal lobbyists.
Sometimes the most obvious is worth reiterating. There is a difference between a department and the policy that falls within its mandate. A department is an instrument. It is put in place to help implement the policy. It is not the policy itself. All departments are

May 11, 1990
Government Orders
administrative instruments for implementing policies and programs.
Unfortunately, some members have forgotten this important distinction. They have proposed amendments that go far beyond the scope of an administrative bill. Ironically, they would be limiting the scope of the department to narrow issues. They would limit the department only to multicultural matters. They and their lobbyist friends would create an ethnic ghetto in the name of providing what they call "precision".
Do we really want to re-open debates that took place in 1988 on the Canadian Multiculturalism Act, an act which was passed unanimously by this House and which embodies our multicultural policy? Who were the members of the opposition listening to then? They were hearing many voices, but listening to only one, a decidedly negative voice-the executive of the Canadian Ethnocultural Council.
Let me remind the House and the Opposition that this organization originally favoured a strong Department of Multiculturalism and Citizenship. But when we did not accede to the narrow, and let me say, self-serving proposals it made to the legislative committee, it changed horses mid-stream, retracting its support.
I suggest to my colleagues across the way that there are some other voices out there that they should be listening to. For example, they should be listening to the Canadian Citizenship Federation, the National Voluntary Organization, national literacy groups from across the country, Harambi Centres Canada, the Committee for Racial Justice, the Association of Multiculturalism, and immigrant serving agencies of British Columbia, to name but a few.
This government believes their views do count. The thousands upon thousands of Canadians who have expressed their support for the establishment of a Department of Multiculturalism and Citizenship should not be ignored. If there is an outstanding characteristic of this department, it is that it is inclusionary. Everyone has a stake in this federal department, just as they do in our nation-building.

The sole purpose of Bill C-18 is to establish the Department of Multiculturalism and Citizenship whose mandate will be to promote equality, fight against racism, and strengthen our common values.

With this bill we in Parliament are seeking to make multiculturalism and citizenship integral parts of the mainstream life of this nation. I believe the gap between our aspirations and reality is slowly narrowing. We have built up an equity in our multicultural policy. We are not starting over again. We are not going back to square one, as members of the Opposition would have us do.
We have rejected the old, tired ideas of the past about what multiculturalism means to Canada. This Department of Multiculturalism and Citizenship will carry out a more meaningful policy. It will help move us one more step forward toward a higher ideal for this country.

The department will relate to all Canadians, men and women alike, for they are all members of our multicultural society and share the binding link of citizenship.
There is no question here of a department solely responsible for multiculturalism nor of a small token department for so-called "ethnic groups". The government simply will not indulge in that kind of cynicism.

The creation of this department follows directly from the vision and the ideals expressed in the Canadian Multiculturalism Act of 1988. As a people we recognize that multiculturalism is a fundamental characteristic of our society. Multiculturalism is essential to an understanding of what it means to be a Canadian.
As well, one of our strongest ties as a people is our shared Canadian citizenship. It is both a symbolic link and a living expression of our Canadian unity.
Canadian citizenship is never a final achievement. The new Department of Multiculturalism and Citizenship will foster a greater sense among all Canadians of the
May 11, 1990

responsibilities that go hand in hand with the rights of our citizenship.
When the Prime Minister announced his intention to set up this new department, he sought the careful balance of multiculturalism and citizenship as characteristics central to our contemporary sense of Canada. He did so with great insight. The Prime Minister recognized that governments cannot live our lives for us. They cannot exclude the Canadian people from their own social policies. Certainly, this is true of multiculturalism and citizenship which are elements central to our being Canadian.
Canadians must judge the new department on its aims and objectives, what it strives to achieve within the context of contemporary Canadian society. I would like to cite some examples, such as enhanced literacy, greater understanding about the value of human rights, more widespread participation in the critically important voluntary sector, fighting racism, and promoting the values inherent in our shared citizenship.
I will tell the House what this department is not about. It is not about confrontations, quotas or regulations. The department's mandate is to work co-operatively within government and with all sectors of our society to build a Canada where there are no barriers, a Canada where each of us as individuals can contribute fully to the prosperity, growth, and development of the country, and where everyone can assume all the rights and responsibilities as citizens of this great land of ours.
The greatest strength of the new Department of Multiculturalism and Citizenship resides in the very ideals that give shape to its mandate. Few countries and few people can claim so many close ties between communities. The department seeks to foster these ties to promote greater understanding among Canadians.
Yes, as Canadians, we do have great expectations for ourselves and for our country.
We must fight racism, the sometimes quietness of racism. I believe the most dangerous kind of prejudice is not necessarily the loudest. We must work to ensure that all Canadians have an opportunity to contribute to society and that they can assume and exercise the rights and responsibilities inherent in our citizenship. We must strive to teach all Canadians, new and old, of the values
Government Orders
which are fundamental to our understanding of being Canadian.
How can ideas as vibrant as these be captured in a static definition? This has eluded our friends across the way.
A new Department of Multiculturalism and Citizenship cannot do it all, of course, but it can help focus our energy. It can assist in making our vision and our hopes possible.
This department is about fairness and equality. It is about our future together. That is the heart and soul of its mission.

The new Department of Multiculturalism and Citizenship will strengthen our previous commitments as expressed in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, the Canadian Multiculturalism Act, and new legislation on citizenship. This country needs the contribution of each and every citizen, and we must ensure that all Canadians are given every opportunity to do their share.
The estimates of the new department are an unmistakable indication of our intentions. They relate to participation, understanding, awareness, and enhancement of our society's basic values. The Department of Multiculturalism and Citizenship will become a key department for the future of the country. The department will not be control- or protest-oriented, but rather dedicated to the fulfilment of the hopes harboured by all Canadians.

I would like to conclude my remarks today by encouraging hon. members to support this bill, and to move it rapidly to its passage.
I urge them to do so for their fellow Canadians. People are what this country is all about. They are all this nation of ours can be. In the end, it is not departments or agencies that are the legacy of an administration or a Parliament, but the human progress that is achieved.
Today, the government is living up to a promise we made to all Canadians, for all Canadians. We do so mindful that there is an even greater promise to keep. We must work together for the day when all our citizens

May 11, 1990
Government Orders
enjoy the full richness of life in our beloved Canada. Only then can we say we are truly satisfied.

Thank you, Madam Speaker. The hon. member for Pontiac-Gatineau-Labelle raised a number of points on which I would like to comment, but unfortunately, we don't have enough time.

I wonder what the hon. member means when he says that certain groups are trying to grind the wheels of social progress to a halt.
He also referred to a definition of multiculturalism. A little further in his speech he asked: What does multiculturalism mean to Canada? I submit that it is up to this member and this government to give us finally a definition of multiculturalism. That is what we have been asking for.
We have been asking the minister and the department to tell us what multiculturalism means to this government. As a matter of fact, we are questioning the commitment that appears to be there when we talk about it. We pay lip-service to it, but what are we really doing?
The hon. member also said that members of the Opposition and the other party are not defending citizenship. I do not know where the member hides himself, but in my riding the almost all the immigrants become citizens. Every chance we have, we talk about Canada. We talk about them choosing this as their country. If they want to become citizens of our country, we are there to help them. I have worked in the community at the grass roots for 20 years. I know what I am talking about.
The hon. member talked about an ethnic ghetto that is being formed. Before too long, the ethnic communities of the country are going to outnumber the francophones and the British who founded it. I do not think we are forming a ghetto in this country at all. I object to anyone saying that the Canadian Ethnocultural Council is trying to form an ethnic ghetto. It represents about 20 or 30 groups in the country. Let us tell the National Italian
Congress of Canada that it wants to form an ethnic ghetto. Let us tell CRARR from Montreal that it wants to form an ethnic ghetto. I strongly object to that suggestion.
I would like the member to explain how a ministry or a department, with no logical objectives, no responsibilities, and no accountability, can help the multicultural mosaic of our country.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF MULTICULTURALISM AND CITIZENSHIP ACT
speechtext: Resuming debate, the hon. member for Saint Laurent-Cartier-ville.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF MULTICULTURALISM AND CITIZENSHIP ACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is too bad there is not a period for questions and comments. The member raised several points that I feel were contentious.

As multiculturalism and citizenship spokesperson with my colleague for Broadview-Greenwood, I welcome this opportunity to take part in the debate today. The government is to be commended for tabling this bill. Creating a Department of Multiculturalism and Citizenship is a positive gestures, reflecting our recognition of the diversity and equality of all Canadians, irrespective of race, nationality or creed.

This new department is a step in the right direction, but for it to be more than a front-and that is what I was referring to-it must be a leader from the start. It is necessary that a senior minister take charge and, also, that part of the staff represent or at least be knowledgeable of the real needs of the different groups it wishes to help. Without clear goals and a good framework, it would be difficult to assess the demands and effectively react, thus the importance of objectives and controls from the start.
Today, almost 40 per cent of the Canadian population is of ethnic origin-that is, not French or British-and this percentage is increasing steadily. Our new multicultural reality is both a major asset and an extraordinary challenge for Canada. It is a major asset, because the entire country can benefit from this multicultural diversity, both economically and culturally.
Canada's future depends on its ability to recognize and promote this Canadian mosaic. Recognizing and encouraging this fundamental characteristic of our country means, in practical terms, that we must develop political mechanisms and programs that will enable Canadian society to establish harmonious interracial relations, based on mutual respect and equal participation.
That is the challenge of Canadian multiculturalism. Failure to meet this challenge would be a serious threat to our future. Imagine what our country would be like if intolerance, racial tension and conflict, were the rule.

Canada cannot afford, if it wishes to stay a country, a rise in tension and intolerance between the different groups living here. It is a new challenge because we are now discovering new minorities and different races all over this country. We must learn to accept and learn from these new groups as they from us. The road towards social harmony is a long one but it is one that the government has accepted to take. Let us stay alert and assure it fulfils its task.

Madam Speaker, while recognizing the importance of a Department of Multiculturalism and Citizenship, I question the potential for action by this department. It seems there are still a number of gray areas in this bill, despite all our efforts in the legislative committee to clarify certain points and suggest amendments. Unfortunately, we did not succeed.
Most issues relating to multiculturalism and citizenship will be the responsibility of a new minister whose duties will include ensuring that the multiculturalism policy announced in the Department of Multiculturalism and citizenship Act is implemented. He must monitor

May 11, 1990
Government Orders
the policies of all departments and federal institutions, which is not made sufficiently clear in the bill.
Madam Speaker, the specific duties of the minister, as set forth in the bill, include to promote national policies and programs with respect to multiculturalism and citizenship; to provide services for the acquisition of citizenship; to promote greater understanding of human rights; and to make grants and contributions in support of special programs for race relations.

The new minister's mandate is a very broad one, so broad that one wonders how it will be possible to control what is to be done effectively in the new department and what is to be done in all other departments affected by the minimum quotas to be respected with regard to hiring people from different minority groups, among other things.

Madam Speaker, while the government is to be commended for increasing funds to promote race relations, I must say that at the same time, the government has disappointed both me and community groups by imposing budget cuts on organizations involved with ethnic groups, native people, the disabled, young people and especially, special-interest groups.
My point is, Madam Speaker, that while overall, the budget for multiculturalism has gone up, the funds for community support and participation have decreased by $400,000 this year. This represents a 15 per cent cut in funding for such groups as the Canadian Ethnocultural Council.

The Canada Ethnocultural Council represents 40 groups across the country. When they bowed down and said: "Yes sir, how high do I jump?", that was fine. The minute they started questioning politics and government policy, they are no longer considered to be a representative group of cultural communities.

These groups act as coordinating and liaison bodies to help the different communities communicate with each other and with the various levels of government.
Madam Speaker, I am also concerned because we do not know whether the obvious trend to limit operating grants for groups will last for one year or more. If it continues, the Department of Multiculturalism will be less effective in fighting racism in Canada. It is important for the department to co-operate closely with these organizations so that it is aware of what is in fact happening, and for that, it is essential that these organizations survive.
Madam Speaker, another point that I consider worth mentioning is the staff of the new department. The present employees to be transferred from the Secretary of State's Department are too few to fulfil the responsibilities of this new department.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF MULTICULTURALISM AND CITIZENSHIP ACT
speechtext: It changes nothing!

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF MULTICULTURALISM AND CITIZENSHIP ACT
speechtext:
Oh! I would like to have an explanation as to how it changes nothing.
Clause 5 of the bill stipulates that the minister's duties are to initiate, recommend, coordinate, implement and promote national policies and programs with respect to multiculturalism and citizenship. This is a big responsibility and the number of people working in this new department and the funds to support them must be increased for it to be effective.
It is also very important that additional staff be of diverse origins and cultures. It is essential that the new department set an example in hiring visible minorities, but it is just as important for those working there to be aware of the issues. They must come from the grass roots and understand the real needs of the communities so that they actually represent what Canada is today.
Madam Speaker, it is essential to hire people who are culturally attuned to multiculturalism and it is also important to provide funds for community programs. It is essential that groups speaking on behalf of cultural communities have sufficient funds to remain a real resource that helps the government in its work.
Madam Speaker, it is also necessary to provide a medium- and long-term budget so that the new department and the various organizations representing groups can take positive action from the start in order to give effective recognition to the mosaic that is Canada in 1990. Above all, we must not have a department with expectations that cannot be met because of budget cuts.
May 11, 1990

Neither must the funds given to the new department come from cuts to associations reflecting the various groups across the country. Both must work together so that the new department meets the challenge it has set itself and for that, the minister must have both the staff and the budget.

Without a budget a department cannot function. With only a short-term budget, projects will be limited and poorly motivated because of a lack of security. A new department, and especially this one, must be guaranteed a long-term budget if it is to be pro-active in today's society and permit all to be treated equally in fact and not merely on paper.
Madam Speaker, the department must not be allowed to become a department of good intentions which pave the road to hell, as they say. It must be an active department. By creating expectations and promising positive action, the government has put it reputation on the line. Now it will have to deliver.
Here is what the minister said in his speech in June, and I quote: "The central responsibility of this department is to strengthen the solidarity of the Canadian people by ensuring that all Canadians participate fully and without discrimination in defining and building Canada's future. This is a time of change and transition in our nation, a time when the evolving cultural and racial diversity of contemporary Canada presents a new image of what we are as Canadians. It is a time when we are seeking to ensure that all Canadians receive fair and equal treatment, that all Canadians have the same chance to participate and to achieve their dreams."
If we really want all Canadians to have the same chance to participate, it is crucial that all citizens have access to current events, so that they can have their say, either through presentations, letters, elections or by any other means. This implies that everyone must be able to read, write and communicate in one of our official languages. That is a major challenge, but it is one the new minister will have to meet early on, if he really wants all Canadians to have the same chance to understand what is happening in our country.
Government Orders
Madam Speaker, to ensure all these pious wishes come true, we feel that, as recommended by a number of groups that appeared before the legislative committee, it would be desirable to have a commissioner of multicul-turalism who would monitor enforcement of the Department of Multiculturalism and Citizenship Act. This position would be similar to that of the Commissioner of Official Languages, and its incumbent would operate on an arms-length basis to ensure his right to criticize.
Madam Speaker, another option would be to have the Canadian Human Rights Commission monitor implementation of multiculturalism and rule on complaints filed with respect to multiculturalism and citizenship, as provided under the Canadian Human Rights Act.
Madam Speaker, our emphasis on the need for monitoring by a commissioner is merely to ensure that in the years to come, under the department or government that happens to be there at the time, there will be positive action, with programs directed towards the future, programs that are people-oriented and that teach the target population.
Not that we have any particular doubts about the effectiveness of the future minister, especially since we don't know yet who it will be. Will there be a new minister? Will it be the Secretary of State again? We also have some concern about responsibilities that have not yet been set out. We are concerned, however, about ensuring continuity between the written word and concrete action, so that all Canadians become aware of a genuine openness in Canada, directed to those who make this country what it is today and what it will be tomorrow, on the eve of the twenty-first century.
Madam Speaker, a tool that has been little or poorly used to promote and understand the differences that make us unique as Canadians is the media, and especially television.
It is essential that what we see on television reflects the multicultural and multiracial reality of the Canada in which we live. It is also very important, Madam Speaker, if we are to have a proper understanding of the needs of the various groups this medium is to represent, to have on staff people of different backgrounds and races, who are aware of the needs and are in touch with these communities, so that the correct image is projected. Once again, by example and education we can discover

May 11, 1990
Government Orders
together the rich resources of this country and those who live in it.
Whatever our background, we are all Canadians and proud of it. That is the reality that should be projected through all the media. It is essential that the government uses wisely the tools at its disposal, so that all Canadians will have the same chance to participate.
Madam Speaker, as I said earlier, creating the Department of Multiculturalism and Citizenship is an important step towards the future, but the government creates expectations it must be able to meet.
To ensure the department's credibility from the outset, Bill C-18, an Act to establish the Department of Multiculturalism and Citizenship and to amend certain Acts in relation thereto, must contain a reference to Bill C-93, an Act for the preservation and enhancement of multiculturalism in Canada. This reference, Madam Speaker, will provide a better framework for the new department by including, for instance, a definition of multiculturalism.
We realize that Bill C-18 is the logical sequel to Bill C-93, since the government wants to create a department. But to avoid misunderstanding or false expectations about the new department, it is necessary to clearly state for whom this department exists, so that its future actions and positions can be better understood.
It is still fundamental to lay the proper groundwork, including the rationale, power and target groups of the new department, so that it starts off on the right foot, whence the importance of reference to Bill C-93. What seems obvious today, which would justify not referring to Bill C-93, will not necessarily be obvious tomorrow. It is always better to have more information rather than less, so that we will have a department that can take its rightful place and meet its commitments.

If the government really does wish to have a new department that will have a positive impact on our society it is important that, from the beginning, the role, mandate, budget and control system be specified, thus avoiding unnecessary mistakes.

While we appreciate the creation of a new Department of Multiculturalism and Citizenship, we remain cautious about its future effectiveness. Since it has such a broad mandate, we will remain on the lookout to see if it will in fact take positive action and have clout in 1990. The government has raised expectations in various ethnic and racial groups. Let us see whether it will keep its promises.

similar to the Official Languages Commissioner. Representatives of citizenship organizations, and I hope my friend on the opposite side who was so critical about admission of citizenship will listen to this because we listened to the representatives of the citizenship organization, wanted a much greater emphasis on citizenship in this bill. We proposed a name change and the toughening up of a number of sections to do this. But the government and the minister were the ones who turned this down in committee, so let us get the facts straight in this House today.
In the Standing Committee on Multiculturalism, which was meeting concurrently with the legislative committee, we worked as an all-party group to get consensus on an all-party definition of multiculturalism. We took the preamble to Bill C-93, so it was not anything new. It was not an invention of myself or anyone else. It was in the act but we were rephrasing it and putting in a slightly tougher wording on the equality aspects. We agreed in the standing committee that this should be presented. The minister would not listen to it. It is ironic that the government at report stage of the bill had to bring in a hundred Tories to vote against the simple definition of multiculturalism. They could have brought in their own definition if they wanted to and we would not have cared. They obviously did not want to strengthen this bill.
I would like to refer the House to our proposed preamble which referred to strengthening the Citizenship Act which provides that all Canadians, whether by birth or by choice, should enjoy equal status and are entitled the same rights, powers and privileges and are subject to the same obligations, duties and liabilities; whereas the Canadian Multiculturalism Act establishes a multicultural policy for Canada, including the requirement that all federal departments and institutions implement this policy; whereas multiculturalism is for all Canadians and is a fundamental characteristic of Canada based on the recognition of the diversity and the equality of Canadians as regards race, national or ethnic origin, colour and religion while recognizing two official languages. Multiculturalism is a government policy commitment designed to preserve and enhance the multicultural heritage of Canadians, to eliminate racism, and to achieve equality for all Canadians.

Madam Speaker, I rise today to address an issue that I am sure is of concern to many members. As the Soviet Union evolves under Mikhail Gorbachev's glasnost a resurgence of anti-Semitism is reaching a dangerous level. The rise of nationalist movements such as Pamyat are of great concern to those of us who are interested in seeing a transition of the U.S.S.R. into a prosperous and tolerant member of the international community.
I would like to express my profound concern for the safety of the Jewish people in the Soviet Union. I urge the Government of Canada to communicate to the Government of the U.S.S.R. to allow those individuals who wish to leave the Soviet Union the opportunity to do so. It is also time that Canada act in a manner consistent with its image as a caring and thoughtful nation.
I urge the Minister of Employment and Immigration and the Secretary of State for External Affairs to staff the Canadian embassy in Moscow with more immigration officers to facilitate the reunification of Jewish families with their relatives in Canada.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to note that the government has decided to renew the Court Challenges Program for another period of five years.
This program provides financial assistance for test cases of national significance put forward on behalf of or by disadvantaged groups and individuals. These cases serve to clarify the language and equality rights of Canadians under the Constitution. In renewing the program the Government of Canada has demonstrated
May 11, 1990

its commitment to the advancement of human rights in Canada.
I am pleased to see that the report of the Standing Committee on Human Rights and the Status of Disabled Persons on the Court Challenges Program has contributed to this positive action on the part of the government. The renewal of the program will be received very favourably by all the groups which appeared before the committee.

Madam Speaker, next week is National Tourism Awareness Week.
Tourism is Canada's fastest growing job creator and by the year 2000 will be the largest industry in the world.
Over 1.2 million Canadians are employed directly or indirectly in tourism at all levels of education and skills, which means that one out of every ten workers in Canada is employed in tourism, and 60,000 businesses generate all or most of their revenue directly from tourism.
Tourism brought $24 billion into the Canadian economy in 1988 and ranked third among foreign exchange earners, surpassed only by the auto industry.
While this vital industry continues to be a leading economic factor, it is also an industry at risk. The goods and services tax will curtail its job growth rate, and our travel deficit continues to grow.
Canada competes world-wide for tourism dollars and marketing is the key. We must ensure that we fight aggressively to keep our share in this industry and to keep Canada competitive in the global tourism marketplace.

Madam Speaker, tomorrow we celebrate National Health Day. This year's theme, "health services, a resource for our community", was chosen to highlight the essential role health services play in society. Service to the community and financial responsibility are the cornerstones of this
vast multifaceted public system that has been established over the years to meet the growing and very diverse needs of Canadians.
I therefore invite all Canadians to join in the activities of this special day that gives us an opportunity to recognize the skills and devotion of thousands of professionals and volunteers who work in the health field and provide the high-quality care that we all enjoy in Canada.
On behalf of the federal government, I wish to thank very sincerely the Canadian Public Health Association and the Canadian Hospital Association, the two organizations that have sponsored National Health Day for several years now.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in spite of all the constructive efforts of Liberal members to make the Conservatives understand that Canadians do not want the GST the government has gone ahead and adopted this regressive and repugnant measure, over of the objections of the Opposition.
Well, Madam Speaker, the fight is not over. Tomorrow, bolstered by thousands of fellow Canadians, Liberal members will rally on Parliament Hill in yet one more attempt to convince the Conservatives that they must immediately drop the GST bill.
Tomorrow, May 12, at noon, Canadians will gather here on Parliament Hill and, given the unpopularity of the Conservatives, we will try again-

speechtext: The time of the hon. member has expired.

Madam Speaker, tomorrow we are celebrating Canada Health Day throughout the country.
This year's theme "Health Services: Our Community Resource" was chosen in recognition of the significant role played by health services in communities throughout Canada. Health services, which are supported by public funds, respond directly to community health needs. Community service and fiscal responsibility are

May 11, 1990
the cornerstones of these important community resources.
I invite all Canadians to join in recognizing the skills and dedication of the thousands of voluntary and professional health care workers who contribute to the high quality of health services that we enjoy in Canada.
On behalf of the federal government, I would like to thank the Canadian Hospital Association and the Canadian Public Health Association for taking the initiative to sponsor Canada Health Day.

Madam Speaker, the Tory government is punishing unemployed workers for attempting to upgrade their job skills by undertaking training programs under Section 26 of the Unemployment Insurance Act.
As of April, 4,000 British Columbians, including people taking training for nursing, child care, computer programming and forest resource workers, have had their UIC discontinued. These include students who are paying their own fees. The government can provide training assistance under existing UIC legislation. There is no need to punish these people because Bill C-21 has not been passed by the Senate.
I call upon the government to restore the training allowance immediately to these 4,000 deserving British Columbians.

speakeroldname: Mr. Michel Champagne (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Forestry)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Forestry
speechtext:
In a few hours, Madam Speaker, we will be witnessing the closing activities of our National Forestry Week.
The purpose of this annual event is to make all Canadians aware of the importance of our forests. They are the income source of 800,000 Canadians and their economic impact is undeniable.
However it has become imperative to stress further the environmental impact of this precious resource. Fortunately, Canadians are ever more conscious of this issue and their positive attitude augurs well for the years to come.
Let us make sure that National Forestry Week is not an event which people forget the minute it is over. Each of us must see to it that showing respect for trees and nature becomes part of our daily activities.
They are our forests, let us look after them.

Madam Speaker, the Canadian Union of Public Employees, Canada's largest union, will be seeking wage increases of at least 8 per cent to 9 per cent to protect workers from the GST.
According to CUPE, these increases include a 3 per cent hike to cover the impact of the GST and another 5 per cent to 6 per cent to allow for inflation.
The government has been working under the assumption that the employees will not seek or will not ask for higher wages as a result of the GST.
Obviously the government's assumption that there will only be a 1.25 per cent inflation increase has flown out of the window. As a result of the GST, for at least another two years, inflation will be higher, interest rates will be higher, and the deficit will continue to increase.
Once again, Canadians will be gathering on Parliament Hill tomorrow at noon to oppose this tax. What is it going to take for this government to put a moratorium on this tax? It takes leadership. Where is it?

Madam Speaker, Canadians do not want higher prices in the stores. Canadians do not want higher interest rates in the future. Canadians want assurances that we are going to have a stable economy next year, particularly when the goods and services tax comes in.
May 11, 1990

Right now the consumer and corporate affairs committee is holding hearings into exactly how we might be able to achieve this, but at the same time a major labour leader is telling Canadians he is going to use the GST as an excuse for major wage demands.
In today's press, the leader of the Canadian Union of Public Employees, Jeff Rose, stated:
We are telling our 377,000 members across the country to factor in a 3 per cent hike for the impact of GST and another 5 to 6 per cent for-inflation.
This is irresponsible on the part of the union. This is exactly what we do not need. This is the kind of fabricated demand which will lead to higher inflation, higher interest rates, higher prices for consumers, and an economy in trouble.
Responsible Canadians call upon our major labour leaders to be responsible and not put their own interests before those of Canada.

Madam Speaker, this morning we awoke to the shocking news and nauseating view of the desecration of a mainly Jewish cemetery in the south of France. This kind of deplorable act, possibly by fringe lunatics or fanatics, is not an isolated incident; it has occurred in my own community in Montreal. People of good will do not accept such acts of racism. When racism raises its ugly head, we all have to fight it. It calls for the world to speak up.
And how sad is the irony in this expression of antiSemitism the very week that world Jewish leaders went to Wansee Villa where officials of the Third Reich met 48 years ago outlining the policy of Nazi genocide. The Jewish leaders declared the forty-fifth anniversary of the defeat of Nazism as a victory for all mankind over this lowest point in man's inhumanity to man.
Leaders of good will around the world should never remain silent in the face of malevolent acts of racism wherever and whenever they occur, for to do so can be mistaken for indifference.
Most Canadians reject the desecration of consecrated land and even in the most challenging of times still share a belief in tolerance, understanding, and respect for basic human rights.

Madam Speaker, just a few minutes ago we heard the chair of the Standing Committee on Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Government Operations attacking the Canadian Union of Public Employees.
It is interesting to note what kind of justice that union can expect to receive from a chair who has attacked it publicly at this time. It throws into question the whole role of the chairs of our standing committees. Obviously the chair of the Standing Committee on Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Government Orders is acting as a spokesman for government policy and is not acting in the interests of all members of Parliament.
In addition, we heard a Liberal member speak in favour of the Canadian Union of Public Employees. However, it was the Liberals who supported the Conservatives in the standing committee, summoning the Canadian Union of Public Employees before that committee and the Canadian Labour Congress.
It is interesting to note that those same groups were denied the opportunity to speak in front of the finance committee in opposition to the GST, another committee-

speechtext: I am sorry, the hon. member's time has expired.

Madam Speaker, for the Canadian Cystic Fibrosis Foundation, 1989 was a year to remember. The discovery of the gene responsible for cystic fibrosis, a genetic disease which affects the lungs and digestive system of young people, was announced by researchers at the Hospital for Sick Children in Toronto. Thanks to these remarkable accomplishments, we can all look ahead with hope and promise.
As a result of the breakthrough, it is hoped that the goal of finding a cure, or effective control, will be achieved much more quickly than was thought possible only a short time ago.
Since this is cystic fibrosis month, it seems appropriate that we reflect on these recent achievements and also salute the Canadian Cystic Fibrosis Foundation, its many volunteers and financial donors who make it possible for

May 11, 1990
Oral Questions
the foundation to contribute approximately $3 million to $4 million annually toward cystic fibrosis research, in addition to supporting clinics for patients and providing information and public education programs.
Congratulations to the Canadian Cystic Fibrosis Foundation.

Madam Speaker, my office has been deluged this week with phone calls from Public Service employees wondering whether they are allowed to participate in a rally on Parliament Hill tomorrow against the goods and services tax.
They are concerned that their jobs may be in jeopardy if they turn up here at noon tomorrow, Saturday, May 12, on Parliament Hill, to tell the government what they think of the goods and services tax.
This symbol of freedom and democracy, this place where the people speak, is already under a shadow, a shadow of excessive use of closure, ignoring the petitions of hundreds of thousands of Canadians, and the arrest of people who come here to speak their mind.
I am telling people that not even this government would dare fire or discipline somebody just for saying what they think about something that is going to affect them and their families every day of their lives.
I urge them to come here tomorrow, Saturday, May 12, at noon on Parliament Hill and let the government know what they think about the GST.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister.
Today, we learned that the top five executives at Canadian National Railways, which is owned by and accountable to the government, last year received wage increases averaging over 18 per cent.
This is the same government that is asking ordinary Canadian workers to bite the bullet on wage increases to help fight inflation.
How can the government be taken seriously when it asks Canadians to exercise wage restraint when top executives of its own Crown corporations are receiving wage increases in excess of 18 per cent? How can the government be taken seriously on this in any way, shape or form?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (President of the Treasury Board):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to clarify for my hon. colleague opposite that the facts that were reported in the story talk about cash compensation. It is not a question of salary. There are bonuses included in here and it is quite confusing.
When I read the article, I have to underline to my hon. colleague that those bonuses for 1988 have been mixed with the 1989 salary levels. In 1988, CN had its best year ever and that is why those increases are there.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the minister's answer is totally unsatisfactory. The executives still got the money. Call it cash, call it compensation, they got the money. How can the government possibly defend these massive increases in the salaries of CN executives when, at the same time, in the same period, ordinary workers at CN got increases of only 4.5 per cent?
Will the government order an immediate salary rollback for these executives, a roll-back to the same rate that it expects Canadians to live with? Will it roll-back these salaries? Yes, or no?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (President of the Treasury Board):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to tell my hon. colleague how these compensation numbers are arrived at.
Under the former government, an independent commission was set up to report so that salaries for Governor in Council appointees would be set in an independent way from government. That is the Burns Commission. The Burns Commission is the one that makes the
May 11, 1990

recommendation both for the salary ranges and for the bonuses to be paid when performance exceeds what has been predicted.
We are following the rules set out by that independent commission that I mentioned. It was initially set up well before this government took power.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, there is an important difference. At the present time, the government is asking ordinary Canadian workers, not to do anything to compensate for the goods and services tax and to hold back their wages so that they will not be adding to inflation. It is a matter of do as I say, not as I do, when it comes to this government.

Madam Speaker, the government keeps repeating that Canadians must tighten their belts but supports massive salary increases for CN's top executives.
Why are the top brass of Crown corporations like Canadian National getting salary increases that, on average, are four times those given their employees and four times the rate of inflation? Will the government immediately demand that CN's top executives make do with salary increases that are in line with those of their own employees, yes or no?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (President of the Treasury Board):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to remind my hon. colleague first of all that we are very conscious of these salary adjustments. We have looked very closely at the performance in that area.
Average actual increases for senior public servants, including deputy ministers, Governor in Council appointees to federal agencies, board and commissions were limited to 4 per cent in 1988, and 4.2 per cent in 1989. That is very much in line with what we have given to the unions throughout the system.

Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Miniser of Finance. The GST is not yet in effect, but the Minister of Finance is already talking about raising the rate. Yester-
Oral Questions
day, he said he had at least a hundred good reasons for raising the rate of this new tax. In fact, the minister raised the manufacturer's sales tax four times: from 9 to
13.5	per cent. Here is my question.
Could the minister be very specific and inform the House today what the GST rate will be in 1992 and 1993? If he cannot, will he make a commitment today not to increase the GST?

Madam Speaker, I think the hon. member is referring to a quote that came out of a press scrum yesterday. I answered that question in the context of what had been done with other countries.
Of the other countries that have a value-added tax, a GST type of tax, about 18 or 19 have made practically no change in the tax. Other countries have made a change in the tax by raising their GST, the value-added tax rate at the same time that they brought down income tax rates. New Zealand is a good example of one of those countries. The United Kingdom is another example. Other countries have raised their tax to finance additional spending.
The only point that I am making, and I will make it again to the hon. member, is that different countries will treat this in a different way. The underlying point that I made in Canada was that any government, regardless of political stripe, will have to justify very carefully any change in the GST rate from 7 per cent.

Madam Speaker, the minister also said yesterday that if workers demand wage increases to compensate for the GST, there will be an increase in interest rates. This is my question.
What happened to the 11.1 per cent interest rate in the minister's last Budget? Today, even without the GST, the Bank of Canada rate is at 13.75 per cent. When will the minister finally realize that his economic policies are a total disaster for this country?

Mr. Speaker, I need only refer to a column that is in The Globe and Mail this morning by Ted Carmichael who indicates very clearly that the GST is a good policy for

May 11, 1990
Oral Questions
Canada and is the answer to a lot of problems that we are facing today.
I have just come back from Washington where I attended the meetings of the International Monetary Fund. The International Monetary Fund is very supportive of the introduction of the GST.
The Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development, the OECD in Paris, also indicates the significance of this tax in improving our competitive position.
If the hon. member is asking why we should change the existing tax, I say that the reason is because it will improve our ability to export into other markets. It will also change a situation where Canadian producers are paying about a third more sales tax than the imports they compete with.
The more obvious question is, why is the hon. member supporting no change in the policy? Why is he supporting the maintenance of a tax that is going to undermine our competitive position, undermine our ability to sell products in other markets, undermine our ability to create jobs in this country, and undermine our ability to get the deficit down? Those are the questions that he should be answering.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. It is interesting that the Leader of the Liberal Party attacked the government for having the workers at CN receive only wage increases of 4 per cent while the senior executives averaged pay increases of over 18 per cent, because the Liberals voted for that back-to-work legislation on August 27, 1987.
The Minister of Finance has allowed extremely high increases for Mr. Crow. He is allowing very high increases for CN. The Conservatives have attacked workers for trying to make up for the increase in the GST.
What justice is there in this country when the corporate elite are receiving pay increases of 18 per cent, 39 per cent, 40 per cent and workers are not allowed to fight for the increase in the cost-of-living?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (President of the Treasury Board):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I can only repeat my earlier answer. The wage increases for deputy ministers and Governor in Council appointees, the senior management of our Crown corporations and the federal public service are exactly the same wage increases that the government has negotiated with our unions.
I will say once again that these salaries were limited to a 4 per cent increase in 1988 and a 4.2 per cent increase in 1989. So I think there is equity in the system and a demonstrable restraint on the part of government in terms of compensation.

Mr. Speaker, when CN vice-presidents receive pay increases of 39 per cent, through cash bonuses or whatever other mechanisms, I would like to see the government negotiate those same increases with workers.
What is the government's economic policy for all employees? Are the rich going to get richer and richer and richer, whereas employees cannot fight the GST? Is that the policy of this government?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (President of the Treasury Board):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, perhaps the hon. member has not understood my answers so far. The wage increases for senior public servants and GIC appointments are exactly the same as those that were given through collective bargaining to all the other employees. It was 4 per cent in 1988, 4.2 per cent in 1989 and that is comparable. I must say that in some groups that were collectively bargained the increases were higher. This is an average. It is an average, though, that applies to everybody.

Madam Speaker, my question is again directed to the Minister of Finance, or the other minister who is getting up in his place. We do not care whether he says it is 3 per cent or 4 per cent on average. The reality is that some senior people, whether it is the Governor of the Bank of Canada or whether it is CN officials, are receiving 39 per cent more.
Answer the question: Where is the justice in this country? Where is any sense of economic management when you are deliberately giving vast increases to those at the top while telling those who work for a wage, which is all they receive, that they should not negotiate to compensate for the increase in the cost of living which is going to result from the GST coming into place?
May 11, 1990

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (President of the Treasury Board):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, that is precisely the reason why the Burns commission was put into place, to have an independent body in the private sector to make recommendations as to compensation in the upper echelons of the federal public service.
We follow the recommendations of the Burns committee. It is a committee that has served this country well over the years. I believe that what they are doing is seeking equity and fairness in the compensation that we offer our senior executives.

Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the President of the Treasury Board who has repeated several times that the government target for salaries for senior government employees is 4.5 per cent.
The president of CN and other senior executives who got an 18.7 per cent increase are also, as executives of Crown corporations, indirectly employees of the government of Canada.
Jeff Rose, the President of the Canadian Union of Public Employees which represents 377,000 Government of Canada employees, has now said that he is telling his membership to look for an 8 per cent to 9 per cent increase because of the effect of the GST.
Is the minister responsible for the Treasury Board prepared to stand in his place today and tell that president that the government will negotiate that 8 or 9 per cent? Or, will he stand in his place and say that in the current circumstances those salary increases of 18 per cent for CN executives and 28 per cent to 35 per cent for the Governor of the Bank of Canada are immoral, wrong, and an act of hypocrisy and will be turned around in the current climate?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (President of the Treasury Board):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to correct somewhat the premise of the question. I never talked about a
4.5	per cent target. I talked about what actually happened back in 1988 and 1989. The increase for that group of public servants and GIC appointments in 1988 was 4 per cent and, in 1989, it was 4.2 per cent.
Those are facts. They are not targets, they are not goals. Those are facts. They are well in line with the compensation generally offered to all employees of the
Oral Questions
federal government. That is what we are monitoring, with the help of independent commissions, to ensure that our employees are paid fairly and equitably throughout the system.

Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the same minister. Surely the minister will understand that there are, among provincial governments, about
400,000	civil servants in the country. Among federal employees, there are another 250,000 civil servants in the country.
Three-quarters of a million civil servants are being told to forget the impact of the GST and to hold their wage increase expectations at about 4 per cent to 5 per cent, at a time when the minister and the government are doling out 18 per cent taxpayer-dollar-increases to senior executives of the CN and, the greatest act of hypocrisy, a 35 per cent increase to the Governor of the Bank of Canada who wants to fight inflation on everybody else's back but his own.
Will the government call in the board of directors of both the Bank of Canada and CN, and direct that those wage increases be rolled back to be consistent with what ordinary Canadians are expected to bear in this time of fighting inflation?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (President of the Treasury Board):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my hon. colleague opposite talks about wage settlements in the provincial sector, in other government sectors, or in the private sector. We have no lessons to take from the group opposite. We have the best record of anybody in the country in exercising responsible wage management and negotiations. We have the lowest rate of wage increases in the public sector and, in comparison to the private sector, we have been doing very well indeed.

Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister and it concerns the unconscionable expenses of the patronage appointees to the board of directors of Ports Canada.
Documents recently obtained from the Department of Transport detailed an absolute orgy of arrogance and abuse, with some directors claiming as much as $35,000

May 11, 1990
Oral Questions
over a period of three months on trips to conventions in Florida and high-priced wining and dining.
How can the minister possibly justify this blatant abuse of taxpayers' money at the very time the government is telling Canadians to tighten their belts and to do with less? How can he possibly justify that?

speakeroldname: Hon. Kini Campbell (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to take the question on behalf of my colleague, the Minister of Transport, who is unable to be here today.
I am advised that the Canada Ports Corporation Board consists of 17 members who, in fact, live in all parts of the country and who are responsible for promoting the use of Canada's major ports. They need to travel extensively to attend board and other meetings and to perform that function of promoting Canada's ports.
Funding for their travel comes from funds provided from the revenues of Canada's major ports, which made a profit last year of $43 million.
Hear, hear!

Madam Speaker, I might as well direct my supplementary question to the President of the Treasury Board, because the Minister of Finance collects it and the President of the Treasury Board spends it.
In response to public outcry at these outrageous expenses, a member of the board said: "Ports Canada made between $50 million and $60 million in profits last year. Unlike other corporations, this one is successful. We can't nickel and dime ourselves."
Has the minister ordered an internal audit into the board's behaviour? In the interim, will the minister issue a set of guidelines to stop this blatant squandering of taxpayers' hard-earned dollars?

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am sure the hon. member would not expect me to make undertakings in the House on behalf of my colleague, the Minister of Transport, but I would be happy to convey to him the hon. member's opinion of these events and his sense of outrage.

Madam Speaker, I must say that you would not know that the last people who put wage and price controls and wage freezes into effect in the country were the Liberals.

However, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. Yesterday in Quebec, the minister said he had a hundred good reasons for raising the GST. Will the minister make a commitment now that he will not raise the GST? Yes or no?

Madam Speaker, I find myself in the unusual position of being able to associate myself fully with the first part of the preamble to the hon. member's question where he expressed surprise at the feigned outrage of the Liberal Party on the matters that have been put before the House today.
On the question of the GST rate, I have responded to that in response to a member from the Liberal Party. That matter came up in the context of what other countries had done. I pointed out that other countries had raised the rate for a number of reasons. Some of them related to spending increases and some of them related to a completely offsetting reduction in their income tax rates. A number of countries, 18,1 believe it is, have made practically no change in their value-added tax rates.
But the underlying point that I made in relation to Canada-and I want to stress this very strongly-is that no government in the future is going to be able to increase the rate on the GST without being able to lay before the Canadian people, in a very clear way, some substantive reasons to support any change in the rate. At this point, we have no intentions whatsoever of making any change in that rate.

Madam Speaker, I thank the minister for being onside with my preliminary comments. I just wish that he had not voted with the Liberals in favour of the six and five program in the past.
The minister and the Bank of Canada have both been trying to sell Canadians on the GST, saying that the tax will have just a one-shot impact on inflation. Does the minister not realize that by refusing any guarantee
May 11, 1990

yesterday he destroys that argument? Does he not see that refusing a guarantee and refusing to say to Canadians that he will not raise the goods and services tax will lead to the very inflationary spiral that he says he wants to avoid?

Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend could contribute to ensuring that the GST rate does not go up in the future by supporting the government on the various proposals to control government spending that it has been making from time to time for the last number of years. Tax rates are related to government spending. If the New Democratic Party was at all concerned about the level of tax rates, it would not be so outrageously irresponsible in proposing increases in spending.

Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. The minister will know that student tuition fees and student debt have been growing throughout Canada at an alarming rate.
Now that the minister has received representations from credible national organizations, such as the Canadian Teachers' Federation, the Canadian School Trustees' Council, the Canadian Federation of Students, and the Canadian Association of University Teachers, pointing out the extremely destructive effects of the goods and services tax on education, will he eliminate the education tax that he is about to impose?
Madam Speaker, there is no tax on education. There is no GST on educational services. That is a simple part of the legislation.

Madam Speaker, I find it increasingly surprising that these credible national organizations disagree with the minister, but that is another question.

Madam Speaker, since the minister refuses to eliminate the GST on education, is he prepared to cancel the
Oral Questions
cuts in transfers to the provinces for education, the same cuts he and the Prime Minister refused to touch? Will he cancel these cuts?
Madam Speaker, I find it very hard to confirm for the hon. member that I will remove a tax that has not been applied. Can he tell me where the tax is applied on educational services-
On books.

-and then we can talk about it. But educational services are not subject to the goods and services tax.
The hon. member has made reference to the transfer payments that we make to the provinces. The transfer payments to the provinces will increase in this coming year in total by 3 per cent. That is exactly the same rate of increase for the total program spending for the Government of Canada. So, we are not asking the provinces to do anything more than what we are prepared to do ourselves.
I would also say that the impact of the changes in the transfer payments to the provinces that were announced in the last budget amounts to less than 1 per cent of their total revenues in year one and a little over 1 per cent in year two. Surely, in the interest of meeting the broad national objective of getting the deficit down, the provinces can adjust to that small amount of reduction in their expected growth of their revenues.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the beleaguered Minister of Transport. I do not know who will answer on the other side today.
The government's blind drive to deregulate the transportation industry has created problems. A Canadian Press story this week indicates that CN's sloppy inspections permitted a rail car full of dangerous acid to travel from Sarnia to Montreal, not once, but twice. Thousands of Canadians were put at risk, including residents of Kingston, Brockville and Cornwall, to name but a few.

May 11, 1990
Oral Questions
What has the minister done to halt these breaches of the regulations?

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I will have to take the question as notice on behalf of the hon. Minister of Transport.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the National Transportation Agency decried CN's inspections and called for a study of railway freight safety across Canada.
Since this recommendation came from an agency headed by his former colleague, the hon. Erik Nielsen, will the Minister of Transport act now to protect Canadians from the foolhardy policies that the government insists on pursuing?

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Madam Speaker, God forbid that, by taking a question as notice, I should prevent the hon. member from having the full benefit of his supplementary. I can assure him that the goals that he suggested are the first priority of this government and I will be pleased to communicate his concerns to my colleague, the Minister of Transport.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Justice. Seventeen constitutional legal experts from law schools across the country have clearly pointed out that the minister's legal justification for the abortion bill is seriously flawed. They have called it legal nonsense and they say the bill creates no entitlement whatsoever to abortion in the country.
Will the minister take the advice of the majority of legal experts in this country on the constitutionality and the appropriateness of this criminal legislation, and will she withdraw Bill C-43?

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, Bill C-43 is before the House. I have no intention of withdrawing it. I would be very pleased to take issue with the report of the legal opinions which was in The Globe and Mail earlier this week. Perhaps the hon. member would like to refer herself to my comments before the Standing Committee on Justice and the Solicitor General yesterday where I did so.

Madam Speaker, these constitutional legal scholars have sent these opinions to the minister. They are from Osgoode Hall, McGill, Western, UBC, the University of Ottawa and the University of Victoria, and they are all telling the minister, in very strong terms, that she is wrong with this legislation. Will she at least refer Bill C-43 to the Supreme Court of Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with respect, the opinions that were proffered-and I have only seen the report in the newspaper about them-did not relate to the constitutionality of this bill at all. According to the newspaper report, they related to the interpretation that I made of their effect with respect to the possibility of provinces to legislate.
I would also point out that the article in The Globe and Mail indicated that one of the opinions solicited happened, in fact, to agree with me. I am not aware of the circumstances under which the opinions were solicited or how the question was framed.
I would also point out that the chairman of the Law Reform Commission of Canada agreed with my interpretation of the effect of the law.
One of the delightful things about being a lawyer is that there is an unlimited number of legal opinions that one can put forward. All statements with respect to the future impact of Bill C-43-and I reiterate again that the issue was not its constitutionality but its impact on the scope of legislation that would then be permitted to the provinces-are, by definition or their very essence, speculative because they will not be resolved until the matter goes before the courts.
I would conclude by saying that in one of the paragraphs of the article-and I am sorry I do not have the clipping with me-it states that the legal academics agree that provincial legislation will be struck down where it is found to be in conflict with the federal law or intended to subvert the intent of a federal criminal law. That was, in fact, the essence of my view and I stand by it.

Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. Canadian manufacturers at the retail
May 11, 1990

level are required to comply with the labelling and packaging act to provide bilingual and metric packaging. Yet American firms are accessing the Canadian market with labels in English only and without metric.
Canadian companies are caught in an unfair situation which will only worsen under free trade and the removal of tariffs. Why will this government not protect Canadian manufacturers from importers who are not complying with the Canadian law?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Blais (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Minister of State (Agriculture)):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Minister of State (Agriculture)
speechtext: Madam Speaker, indeed people have complained several times that imports were treated differently. I must say that since then, with my colleague, the Minister of National Revenue, we have set up teams to ensure that these products from abroad comply with Canadian laws. We are improving the situation, but our market is increasingly global. Things like that can happen. But I can assure you that since the manufacturers' association and the retailers' association communicated with us, we have taken measures at the border with my colleague, the Minister of National Revenue, to deal with the situation, which has improved since then, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, the minister should know that in a letter of April 17 the national organizations which are in place to protect the Canadian retailers are saying it is not working. The minister should know that customs officers do not go around opening boxes at the border to look at the packaging and labelling on the products. They only check to make sure the proper papers are filled out.
Canadian manufacturers are fed up with spending money to conform with the act while their American counterparts are ignoring it. Is it not time this law was enforced? Is it not time that this government stood up for Canada instead of the United States?

ensure that the law and regulations are clearly enforced. We have an interdepartmental committee that worked on it.
