speechtext: At eleven o'clock there were nine minutes remaining in the intervention of the hon. member for Vancouver East.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF MULTICULTURALISM AND CITIZENSHIP ACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as I was saying, the minister refused to add a preamble as a context for Bill C-18. He also refused our amendments, stating that the department and the minister are responsible for implementation of the multiculturalism act. The minister has the duty to work toward the elimination of racism and discrimination in all aspects of Canadian life.
In a later section referring to implementation of employment equity for minorities, a Liberal amendment to establish a commissioner of multiculturalism and our alternate proposal to monitor through the Human Rights Commission also were turned down. At report stage we tried again to include more limited amendments, and once again the minister refused them and offered no improvements himself. Ironically he brought in 100 Tories to vote down my simple definition of multiculturalism.
Because the government resisted any improvements to Bill C-18 and offered no improvements itself and because of budget cuts for funding of multicultural programs which have taken place over the last year, we can only conclude that the government is interested in token political gestures toward multiculturalism. A new Department of Multiculturalism and Citizenship will have no real clout to implement multicultural policy, and the minister will have no influence in cabinet or with other colleagues to influence necessary changes because there was nothing added to this bill to give it teeth and to give a clear mandate to the minister.
May 11, 1990

We were told by the minister that the new department will have no additional resources but merely will have present personnel transferred from the Department of Secretary of State. It will have responsibility for literacy and voluntary action as well as human rights, multicul-turalism and citizenship, which is quite a tall order. Although there would be the cost of a new director and support staff, we wonder where this funding is coming from in as much as community groups have been cut back so drastically.
This refusal to improve Bill C-18 has been disappointing to us. It must have been even more disillusioning to persons who are working in front-line programs and as advocates for a strengthened multicultural policy in Canada.
Over the past year since this bill was introduced there have been severe cut-backs in funding to advocacy groups, a discontinuation of the citizen instruction and language training program, and a complete emasculation of heritage language programs which are basic to the transmission of culture. A federal funding total of $4.1 million was removed from these programs. These are programs that teach 60 different heritage languages to
140,000	in 850 community schools across Canada.
At the same time, ironically, the minister of trade was given $14 million to try to teach Pacific Rim languages to adults. Does this make any kind of sense? Does this show that the multicultural minister has clout to get money for languages? Indeed it does not, and it bodes very poorly for a future department.
However, I would like to commend the minister for one thing he has done. He has consistently stated that funds for race relations programs are his priority, and I agree. This is an urgent concern in Canada. I only wish that he would support existing groups that have this as their goal.
Why has he refused funding for advocacy groups and refused the request of 40 organizations for funding of a media watch project that was deliberately targeted to deal with racism, images and so on in the media, which is very important in this field? Why has he instead decided generously to fund a politically appointed advisory com-
Govemment Orders
mittee? Why has he very secretly, recently through his personal staff, set up a new hand-picked race relations network, which is competing with existing groups?
It was evident in the comments of the spokesman for the minister this morning that this government and this minister are threatened by advocacy groups who have in their mandate an obligation to try and work toward the improvement and the implementation of multicultural policy and the elimination of racism. They think that if they establish new groups, appoint their own political appointees, have complete control over what they say, and have everyone say "yes, yes, you have wonderful programs, to the minister", this is the way to go. This is no commitment to democracy. It is certainly not a sound way to operate a multiculturalism department. I do not know what the minister is afraid of.
The first annual report of the Multiculturalism Act which was tabled a couple of months ago is disappointing. It describes various multicultural programs quite adequately, but it does not really get at the meat of the operation of the Multiculturalism Act, which is to try to influence and change federal policies and the policies of federal departments and institutions, to promote greater equality, to promote the elimination of systemic discrimination, and to promote multiculturalism. This is the main goal of the Multicultural Act. There is nothing in that report that allows us to know what has been done between departments or with federal institutions, if anything at all has been done.
The minister of a new Department of Multiculturalism and Citizenship should be the lead minister to act as a catalyst to bring about institutional and attitudinal change in all our government systems. This is what we want. It is analogous to the role of the Minister responsible for the Status of Women whose job it is to monitor and promote sexual equality in all aspects that come under federal jurisdiction. This is the kind of thing that should have been spelled out in Bill C-18.
Several examples over the past year come to mind where the minister could have influenced public policy and institutional change in government. I do not think he took an active enough stand. The first was multiculturalism in the media. We had a number of incidents brought forward of concerns about stereotyping and the insensi-

May 11, 1990
Government Orders
tivity, particularly of the CBC Crime Connection program and Disparaitre on Radio Canada.
Did the minister or his staff do anything constructive to get to these networks and to CRTC to make sure that we have a better way of monitoring and ensuring multiculturalism in the media?
The question of hatred propaganda. The minister spoke out against racist pins from Alberta, but he really did nothing to meet with ministers to bring in new legislation or tougher restrictions under the Criminal Code. I doubt if he talked to the Attorney General about the question of Sikhs and turbans in the RCMR
The question of an advocacy role, a pro-active role by the minister in entrenching multiculturalism as a fundamental characteristic of Canada in our Constitution, is vital. The minister should have been out front and foremost to do something about this matter.
Also I referred to employment equity. The minister's own department is lacking in this regard since it has only one visible minority person in a senior position.
I would like to go on and on, Mr. Speaker, but you are telling me that my time is up. I wish I had more time to talk about citizenship. I want to say we are very disappointed in this bill. We are disappointed in the defensiveness of the minister who was completely inflexible and would not bring in any changes of his own. We wanted a strong department of citizenship and multiculturalism.
Bill C-18 could have been an effective vehicle to promote a truly multicultural Canada with equality for all Canadians. We regret that it is so limited. We will not oppose this bill because we want a department. We hope in future years it will be improved, but we cannot endorse this very unsatisfactory bill with any enthusiasm at all.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF MULTICULTURALISM AND CITIZENSHIP ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise and speak on this particular bill in the House today. I believe that Bill C-18, an act to establish the Department of Multiculturalism and Citizenship merits our support, but it is flawed.
There are some very real major problems which I would like to identify so that we can do something constructive about them when the opportunity arises.
There is a certain amount of cynicism about the bill. Some people are wondering whether it is a symbolic effort on the part of the government in response to a group of Canadians who have often been denied, and perhaps not treated as equitably or with as much sensitivity as could have been exercised.
Of course Canadians generally are really quite knowledgeable about the smoke and mirror competency of this government on a number of issues. There is often much glitz and puffery in everything that it undertakes. Therefore there is nervousness; there is cynicism. It is really unfortunate because I think fundamentally it is an issue that is particularly important in Canada as we know it today.
I want to review just briefly a bit of history. Both parties are often most anxious to point out Liberal lack
Government Orders
of achievements. I would hope that, before this debate is over, they could commend the Liberal Party for some of the initiatives that it has taken in the past with respect to multiculturalism.
It was in 1971 that the Liberal government introduced a multicultural policy, and I shall quote three of the objectives that were brought forth at that time:
1.	To support all of Canada's cultures, by assisting, resources permitting, the development of interested and needy cultural groups.
2.	To assist members of all cultural groups to overcome cultural barriers to full participation in Canadian society.
3.	To promote creative cultural encounters and interchange among all groups in the interest of national unity.
It was in 1982 that the Liberals took another first step. At that point in time, the concept of multiculturalism was sufficiently entrenched to warrant recognition in Section 27 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms of the Constitution Act, 1982. I think that is a historical moment of some significance.
Mr. Speaker, you will perhaps recall that these Liberal initiatives were congruent with the United Nations subcommittee on the protection of minorities and the prevention of discrimination, a committee that gained prominence because of the human rights issues that were surfacing at the time. The point to be made is that the Liberals undertook some very important initiatives, and this is an attempt to continue to develop those policies. In that sense, they are truly laudable.
As I indicated initially, what has happened is that there is some nervousness out there because people are wondering if this is a symbolic gesture. Why do they ask if it is a symbolic gesture? Everyone who follows the proceedings of the House knows that there have been substantive and substantial cuts in the area of multiculturalism. In light of that fact, why is this being promoted? There is no provision for a commissioner who will ensure that the policy is going to be enforced, that the various initiatives which are going to be undertaken and the objectives that have been set will be realized.
Is it real? Is it serious? Is it really a commitment? Some people will know that there was a rather harsh cut to the citizenship and language instruction agreement. It penalizes new Canadians who want to learn one of our two official languages.

May 11, 1990
Government Orders
Another point that has made people cynical and nervous about this whole initiative is that there have been no changes allowed. If the government is truly serious about this initiative why has it not allowed even a minimum of change?
I should point out, as well, that there is no definition of multiculturalism. When we talk about multiculturalism, are we talking only about people who come to Canada from different language backgrounds? Are we also including people of religious backgrounds?
We all know that there are cultures and various socio-economic groups. For example, the poor have a culture. Are we including the culture of women, men, the elderly, youth, the west, the Atlantic provinces, the north, Quebec, Ontario? What do we mean by "multicultural" or "multiculturalism"? There is a suspicion that it is not known what is meant. There is a further suspicion that it is not even known what culture in itself really is, because we are cognizant that there are many definitions out there.

Is this a purely symbolic gesture? Is this a genuine commitment to a group that deserves some special consideration? Why were cuts made in the budget for multiculturalism? Why is there no definition of the term itself? Why is there no commissioner to ensure the objectives are met and, if they are not met, to ensure these deficiencies are identified so that we, in Parliament, can try to correct them?
Where will we take the staff to fulfill that new department's mandate? Will they be civil servants? I have nothing against that. But will these people have the knowledge needed to enable the department to meet its objectives? The basic question is this: Is this only a token gesture or is it a real initiative? You probably remember the TV add about a certain hamburger chain where the lady was asking: "Where's the beef?" With this bill, many persons ask the same thing: "Where's the beef?"

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF MULTICULTURALISM AND CITIZENSHIP ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased today to deal with this important legislation the purpose of which is to establish the Department of Multiculturalism and Citizenship.
Canada has always been a country that has welcomed people from all over the world who come here seeking freedom, peace and properity.
From the very first French, Irish and Scottish immigrants to the post World War arrivals of European immigrants, and the recent waves of Asian nationals, we have all found in this country a place where we can make our dreams come true.
Like thousands of immigrants who have become Canadian citizens, my family and I are very grateful to Canada and Canadians for accepting us as brothers and for allowing us to fully participate in the life of our community, our city, our province and our country.

I feel that the most concrete way in which we can express our gratitude is to pursue an active role in the country we have chosen. We want to see progress toward greater harmony and prosperity. Our objective is to create a Canada which reflects the ideals and ambitions of its citizens.

As a member of one of Canada's ethnic communities, was able, like many others, to bring to this country a wealth of culture, tradition and expertise which undoubtedly contribute to a large extent, not only to the specific character of Canada, but also to its unique social and economic vitality. Clearly, stronger, more vibrant and more dynamic ethnic communities mean a stronger and more productive Canada.
For instance, Canada already benefits from the fact that it can dialogue and negotiate with the rest of the world in both its official languages. But when it taps the linguistic wealth of its cultural communities, it can readily have access to Europe and Asia which are among the most valuable markets in the world.
But in order to achieve the ambitious goal of building a Canada for the 1990s which accurately reflects its citizenry, we must first develop a successful dialogue, not only among the founding nations of this country but also its various cultural communities which, over the years, have contributed to the richness of the Canadian mosaic.
May 11, 1990

Mr. Speaker, this dialogue between the various components of our society must be based on mutual knowledge and understanding of our diversity, and even our difference.
The hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Turner) expressed this notion so well when he said that there is no majority in Canada anymore, and that one way or another, we are all members of a minority.
Once we have perceived and accepted this reality, it becomes much easier to develop a cultural dialogue and to accept others as equals.
Fighting racism, harmonizing diversity, developing a consensus in spite of differences, providing real equal opportunities represent tough challenges for any country or people.
A recent study done in the United States shows that, despite the noble battles fought by great black leaders such as Martin Luther King and our perception of progress, racism is almost as prevalent today as in the sixties. In some regards, it may be less visible than when segregation was legal but its practical consequences remain about the same. Unfortunately, Canada is far from immune from this social cancer.
By the year 2000, three Montrealers out of five will be of ethnic background. We are already almost half and half. It means that Canadians of every origin, particularly those living in large centres, must quickly adapt their mentality and behaviour to the reality of minorities, especially visible minorities.
It will take time, energy and above all tolerance.
We also need moral and political leadership. We are no longer satisfied with symbolic gestures, token appointments and bandaid solution.

The present government has clearly not understood Canada's multicultural reality of the 1980s and understands even less the coming reality of the 1990s. Despite the electoral promises of 1984 and 1988, the situation today has not improved. The lack of government direction has produced nothing but stagnation, confusion,
Government Orders
and, in my opinion, a deterioration which will sooner or later heighten social agitation.

In order to enhance its image vis-a-vis the cultural communities, the government has tabled a bill on multi-culturalism.
Instead of giving multiculturalism the same support as that given to bilingualism by the Official Languages Act, the bill introduced by this government merely sets the legislative framework for existing programs and extends the principles of multiculturalism to the various governmental branches.
This fooled no one, neither Canadians nor the representatives of our cultural communities.
The Tories are looking for the ethnic vote, but their lack of vision of a strong, united and multicultural country is obvious. This government is putting through a bill regarding multiculturalism and establishing a Department of Multiculturalism and Citizenship while, at the same time, making cutbacks in the heritage language programs.
How can multiculturalism be promoted in Canada when the means to achieve that goal are been cut?
It is the same with official languages. The government introduced and amended an existing act but did not implement the regulations, making the act inoperative.
The Conservative Party is nothing but a political party, a government without vision, without a cause and with no backbone.

The same half-hearted approach was taken by the government in the area of appointments. With seemingly impressive numbers, the government claims to have treated cultural minorities well in this regard. However, looking closely at the appointments, they have been at low levels in crown corporations and the bureaucracy, and often in strictly advisory organizations.
Canada's cultural communities deserve better. To everyone's benefit, we should be able to find Canadians of ethnic backgrounds involved in all sectors, in decisionmaking roles at the highest levels of the bureaucracy, right up to the presidency of crown corporations.

May 11, 1990
Government Orders

Everything has yet to be done. And we certainly cannot rely on the conservative government to expand on the measure. It has proven its incapacity to see the changes in our society and to respond fairly and with compassion to the needs of Canadians of all origins.

I am proud to be Canadian, and I am proud to be a part of a cultural community. I am also proud to be associated with a political party which has always been conscious of Canada's multicultural reality and which has never hesitated to reinforce and develop the role of our communities in the Canadian mosaic.
Canada is a multicultural society made up of native peoples, francophones, anglophones, and ethnocultural groups and all institutions should reflect this.
When I see the current discord on both sides of the language issue it makes me sad. My Canada is a generous, tolerant, and compassionate country. If the language and the culture of the French minority in Canada and of the English minority in Quebec cannot be preserved and promoted, how can we expect that the ethnic languages and cultures will be preserved and promoted. Every time we attack and diminish the value of multiculturalism we increase assimilation and that is not the Canadian way of life.
Canada is a model society in the world, the best country in the world. Regardless of our origins, let us work to keep this country together, living together and recognizing and accepting our differences. It is the way the rest of the world will live in the year 2000. We should work toward that objective and give our example to the world as we have for the last 150 years.

Madam Speaker, Canada stands for tolerance, generosity and compassion. Canadians can live together in spite of their differences.
This new department must promote Canadian unity and the Canadian way of life if Canada is to survive.

Madam Speaker, I appreciate my colleague's compliments and I thank her for allowing me to develop my thoughts on this question.
Canada is a mosaic. The only way to succeed is for us to accept our differences, to recognize our cultural traditions and differences, and to try to live together in harmony. For 150 years this country has stayed together, but lately we have a serious problem. I do not want to enter into the Meech Lake Accord debate because I think it divides us and I would like to speak on things that unite us.
For example, a couple of weeks ago on a national television program, The Journal, I saw people walking on the Quebec flag, burning things, and saying things. When we show that on national television, there is an impact. I know that makes news and the journalists are looking for very appealing events. But many people who watched that program were given the impression that English
May 11, 1990

Canada thinks that way toward French Canada. I strongly believe that that is wrong.
The government says: "We do not have to give CBC a unity mandate." We have to find something to keep the country together and we should use our institutions like the CBC. The departments need a goal to keep the country together which is not an easy thing.
It is almost the year 2000 and we can see what is happening in the Soviet Union and Europe. We are already together. In order to succeed, and to continue to give an example to the rest of the world with our way of living together-celebrating our differences and loving the same country, with different perspectives and different priorities-we should all be Canadians. I believe that the government has to show the leadership.
For political reasons, the government has not shown the leadership needed to keep the country together. We have no cause. Why should Canada stay together? We have to show leadership. We cannot keep the country together only by economic aid. There has to be a reason to be Canadian. Quebec should not stay within Confederation because only it benefits economically. If that is the only reason for Quebec staying in Confederation, one day or another, when Quebec has a stronger economy, it will say: "Canada, we do not need you anymore. We are going to leave."
To stay together, Canada has to have a cause. It has to represent something and, as national politicians, the federal government has to give that kind of message and show leadership. That is the only way we can achieve national unity in the country.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to rise and support the principle of Bill C-18.
At the outset, I would like to make perfectly clear that, because of the refusal of the minister to entertain reasonable improvements to the proposed legislation during committee debates, I have some serious concerns about the adequacy of the legislation.
The bill establishes a new department of multicultur-alism and citizenship following the earlier Canadian Multiculturalism Act which, in itself, establishes objectives for multiculturalism policy in Canada. Although the new department will have the power over most matters
Government Orders
relating to multiculturalism and citizenship, and also the responsibility to enforce implementation of our multicultural policy, the proposed legislation is lacking in many specifics.
My colleagues and I reluctantly support Bill C-18. We whole-heartedly support the principle, but we do feel that the current legislation fails to adequately address the need for a true and vital program of multiculturalism in Canada. That has been a policy of the New Democratic Party for some time.
The bill requires specific improvements imperative in order to establish an agency that would carry out the objectives of the federal policy on multiculturalism. There are several concerns which we continue to have about the particulars of the legislation, such as the questionable ability of the new department to carry out its mandate and objectives.
For example, the present staff members who are to be transferred from the Department of the Secretary of State are simply insufficient to carry out the expanded responsibilities of this new department with its enhanced mandate. Extra staff members with very diverse backgrounds will be needed. It is imperative that staff members who are hired are sensitive to the dynamics of Canada's cultural mosaic.
It is critical that there are sufficient funds available for the deployment of those community-based multicultural programs. If not, then the new department will simply be a form of window-dressing, another example of political tokenism which has been the hallmark of this administration.
My colleague from Vancouver East has spoken eloquently about the cuts and about the needs which are not addressed in this present bill. For example, multicultural organizations have been cut over a three-year period, I believe, by some 50 per cent.
We were very concerned to hear that funds for the citizenship instruction and languages textbook program had been slashed by 50 per cent in 1989, and that the program is slated to be eliminated this year.
These are government initiatives that are simply going in the opposite direction. They are the antithesis of a strong multiculturalism policy.

May 11, 1990
Government Orders
The minister knows full well that the act states the obligation to promote an understanding of the value of Canadian citizenship, and to encourage the participation in the social, cultural, political and economic life of Canada. But how can the minister promote these lofty ideals when his government has in fact slashed the very foundations needed to implement those same programs?
When this bill was first introduced in the spring of 1989, we felt that it was more of a housekeeping measure rather than one which set forth a specific mandate to administer the multicultural act in Canada. My New Democratic colleagues at that time felt that the bill should define specifically multiculturalism, and that it should lay out specifically ministerial responsibilities to implement the policy of multiculturalism in our federal institutions. This bill fails to do that.
Since this bill was debated at second reading last fall, several things have changed which weakens our support for what could have been a very good piece of legislation.
First, in committee, the minister refused to allow reasonable amendments to this bill which would have strengthened it considerably. The suggested amendments included the specific role of the minister and the department in enforcing multiculturalism in federal institutions, a specific reference to the elimination of racism in Canada, the provision for employment equity and the monitoring of the agency by a non-governmental body.
In addition, the budget of the government has made drastic cuts to Secretary of State funding for multiculturalism. These cuts, as I have mentioned already, seriously undermine the ability of our community-based programs and our advocacy groups to function accordingly.
We have seen further cuts to advocacy groups such as the Canadian Ethnocultural Council and the citizenship language training programs, while at the same time the government has been dumping millions of dollars into the construction of a heritage language institute. Here again the government prefers to create expensive central institutions rather than fund worth-while community programs that are so badly needed across Canada.
The minister had an opportunity in committee to make these reasoned changes that are necessary to create a truly workable piece of legislation, one which New Democrats could unconditionally support, but he refused to do so. He refused to give himself the mandate that is so clearly needed to really make things work.
Thus it became apparent that the bill was really window-dressing, and window-dressing is simply inadequate with such an important issue.
New Democrats firmly believe that equality rights must be the primary objective of any policy of multiculturalism in this country. Long before my New Democratic colleagues and I had the privilege of serving in this Chamber, leaders such as J. S. Woodsworth, J. Coldwell and Tommy Douglas spoke out strongly and eloquently about prevailing injustices toward Canada's ethnic minorities. They spoke out about the long history of violations of basic human rights which, regrettably, are an indelible part of Canada's history.
We fought with vigilance the shameful and brutal treatment of our Japanese citizens whose lives were literally ripped apart and whose pride of Canadian citizenship and identity were torn asunder when they were humiliatingly interned during the Second World War. Canada has only recently recognized the need to redress this national crime against our Japanese citizens.
We have pressed for the need for full recognition of our aboriginal peoples, including the right of self-government and the need for a negotiated settlement of native land claims.
We continue to protest the injustices in our present immigration policies. We continue to deplore the systemic discrimination in employment against visible minorities in this country. We continue to fight against the growing intolerance in the incidents of racism in Canada.
Whether or not it is expressed in our Constitution, multiculturalism is a fundamental characteristic of Canada. More than one-third of Canadians come from origins which are not aboriginal. They are not French or English. Their numbers are increasing rapidly.
Together these non-indigenous groups form the largest segment of the Canadian population. In many communities out west, particularly in the Vancouver area, for
May 11, 1990

example, non-English, non-French descendants are actually the majority. In recent years people have come in increasing numbers from Asia, the Caribbean, the Middle East and from many Latin American countries.
Canada has truly become a rich and colourful mosaic, a celebration of culture diversity rather than a homogeneous melting pot as is evidenced in our neighbour to the south.
This accelerating pace of ethnocultural change has not come without its costs. According to official pieties, Canada was born and raised in the spirit of cultural pluralism. Its culmination is the present policy on multi-culturalism. Would that we were born to such a perfect world. Unfortunately, the demons of racial and cultural prejudice have never quite been exorcized from Canadian society.
Incidents of racism and intolerance are etched deeply in our history. For that matter, they are increasingly easy to find in the headlines today, from Alberta-made posters decrying turbaned mounties, to the skinhead rallies in Toronto; from increased hostility toward Hong Kong immigrants in the Vancouver area to growing tensions towards east European immigrants in the mari-times.
The growing tensions are symptomatic of something much deeper and very threatening. At their heart lies the discriminatory hierarchy that differentiates among Canadians and treats some of our citizens as little better than outsiders. Exposure of institutionalized racism in our justice and in our police systems, such as the wrongful imprisonment on a murder charge of a young Indian, Donald Marshall, and the evidence exposed in Manitoba's aboriginal justice inquiry reveal all too clearly the dark side of our national soul.
Canadian petitions to prevent the RCMP from accommodating orthodox Sikh requirements for dress are indeed profoundly disturbing, particularly when one cuts through the misguided arguments of Canadian tradition and finds that we are left with the most painfully frequent argument that Sikhs and their traditions are simply "unCanadian". "Let them take their foreign paraphernalia and go home" is the rallying cry of a vocal faction of our Canadian citizens.
Government Orders
The searing racial intolerance of this argument takes us as a nation a long way from our avowed belief that Canada is among the world's most tolerant of countries.
It seems likely that opportunities for racism and growing intolerance to other ways of life are likely to grow as the composition of Canadian society becomes increasingly diverse. It is symptomatic of a reaction to an accelerating pace of change that will see within the next two decades 20 per cent of the populations of our major cities belonging to non-white minorities.
In conclusion, one hopes that there is no half-way position in human rights. Either we accept the proposition that no race, religion or culture is intrinsically better than another, or we will continue to act and to react in ways that are hypocritically at variance with our declared pluralistic and democratic principles.
We have a lot of work to do to ensure that Canada remains a country recognized globally as a tolerant nation. Canadian norms are multicultural and pluralistic. There are many equally valid ways and equally legal and productive ways of being Canadian. That is our reality.

Madam Speaker, my colleague raises a very legitimate point, one that I had touched on but perhaps not embellished.
The biggest concern that we have with the current legislation is simply the fact that, again, we are dealing with the concept of window-dressing. We are attempting to demonstrate that we are creating an institution which is going to do the job it has set out to do. In fact no piece of legislation, no created department, no created mandate can do the job if the funding is not there at the community level.
It is one thing to pump millions of dollars into creating central institutions, which this government is wont to do. The reality of the problem, in terms of promoting a workable policy and mandate for multiculturalism across Canada, is to put the funding in at the community level for the very programs that are needed in language training of our new citizens and in helping the many community advocacy groups which so desperately need help.
The simplest way to look at it is to consider the analogy of the initial cuts of some $1.6 million to women's programs. While cutting those very necessary community based programs, the government somehow miraculously was also able to justify spending the equivalent amount of money, some $1.6 million, for upgrading the Senate chamber. When we look at it in terms of priorities, it is very obvious that the government is very narrow-minded in determining where its priorities should be.
We say that the funding priorities have to be at the community level and have to be put into the programs that are required in order to make this kind of legislation really workable.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF MULTICULTURALISM AND CITIZENSHIP ACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I too am very pleased to stand today in support of Bill C-18, which is an act to establish the Department of Multiculturalism and Citizenship.
Although the bill is lacking in strength, the current legislation is eminently better than what we have today. It is the appropriate way to move.
The main purpose of the bill is to establish a Department of Multiculturalism and Citizenship. Under that heading there are many areas for which the department will be responsible. It makes me wonder whether, with the projected budget for the 1990-91 estimates of $155,000, just how it is going to achieve all of the goals that it has set out in the guidelines.
I look at the Department of the Environment and the budget estimates that were set up for it and I see the same situation. I do not know why the government tries to set up a new department and allows the estimates to come from each department having each department competing for the same dollar. It makes it very difficult for the minister of that department to achieve his goals or to arrive effectively within the projected guidelines of the department.
The focus of Bill C-18 is on the machinery of government. The new department will consist of five branches at departmental headquarters. They will be multiculturalism, citizenship registration and promotion, literacy, voluntary action, and human rights. We all realize that every one of those areas is an area that certainly requires a tremendous amount of compassion and assistance, not just from members of Parliament but from all Canadians.
Since 1971 the Canadian multicultural policy has evolved. I am very pleased and proud to say that it was enunciated by a Liberal government. The main purpose of the policy was to support all of Canada's cultures to assist the development of interested and needy cultural groups, resources permitting; to assist members of all cultural groups to overcome cultural barriers to full participation in Canadian society; to promote creative cultural encounters and interchange among all groups in the interest of national unity; and to assist immigrants to our country in the acquisition of one of Canada's official languages so to become full participants in Canadian society.
That is pretty heady stuff, but very necessary. Yet there is not the teeth in the bill to achieve all those things. There is not the funding provided in the bill to achieve all those things. They are very necessary if we are to maintain the cultural mosaic that we have here in
May 11, 1990

Canada in which we all live together, where there are many Canadians like myself who were born of Canadians, but an equal number of people who are not Canadian born have adopted Canada as their country.
As immigration continued through the 1970s and 1980s the policy of mulliculturalism took root within the many ethnic communities of Canada. By 1982 it had become sufficiently entrenched to warrant recognition in Section 27 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
International developments and progress in the area of human rights and fundamental freedoms helped the policy of multiculturalism take root. At the United Nations the Subcommittee on the Protection of Minorities and the Prevention of Discrimination gained prominence through its work.
The Canadian policy of multiculturalism, with its emphasis on citizen participation, human rights and cultural diversification, matched a variety of goals established by the United Nations to foster tolerance and understanding. In addition, multiculturalism was also intended to promote national unity and help better define a national identity. Thus the policy of multiculturalism as established by Liberal governments met both domestic and international goals.
What seemed like a policy without flaw was placed under increased strain throughout the latter part of the 1970s and 1980s. Racism manifested itself with increased frequency, and the rapid growth of ethnic communities led to criticism of multiculturalism on the grounds that the policy did too little or too much to help immigrants and thus left them in cultural "ghettos".
The Conservative government enacted the Multiculturalism Act again in 1989 when Bill C-18 was introduced in the thirty-fourth Parliament. Conservative action on multiculturalism is in part an attempt to make inroads into a substantial voting block with a high level of political participation. These groups have provided longstanding support for the Liberal Party. Whether Conservative policies are eroding the support is open to speculation.
Government Orders
My party, the Liberal Party, endorsed the concept of a separate department of multiculturalism in the 1988 election platform. At second reading of Bill C-18 the party again supported the concept but expressed reservations about this bill and suggested amendments in committee. At third reading the party supports the notion of a separate department but still has serious reservations about this bill.
Although the establishment of a department is a step in the right direction, the lack of guaranteed funding to each specific branch within the department could very well cause problems if each branch has to compete more vigorously for a decreasing amount of money. I mentioned that earlier and I compared it to the new Department of the Environment where each department puts forward its request. They talk about the issues. They are all competing for the same dollar.
Another weakness is that the bill fails to provide an adequate enforcement mechanism, such as a commissioner of multiculturalism who would monitor and enforce the proper delivery of multicultural policy.
While the concept of the bill is a welcome one, this government's actions are large symbolic. This bill could have been much stronger. It could have established institutional organs to help better define and enforce multicultural policy, guaranteed levels of funding for the department, and a policy path that would expand the impact of multicultural policy.
Hence, multicultural policy would not service a few client ethnic groups but rather educate all Canadians of our multicultural heritage about the principles of racial and religious understanding and about the concept of national unity and the need to develop a Canadian identity while retaining one's ethnic culture.
On March 31, the Conservatives terminated the citizenship and language instruction agreement. This agreement provided textbooks to the provincial and territorial governments for half the class instructional costs and up to the full amount of costs for citizenship textbooks. How is national unity to be promoted and how does Canadian identity become defined when the federal government withdraws from progress that could strengthen both?
Quite recently I attended a meeting of the heritage schools in the Ottawa-Carleton area in which my riding is located. I cannot remember the exact number, but there were at least 20 heritage schools operating in this area. They have had drastic cuts in funding. These

May 11, 1990
Government Orders
people were trying to retain a small portion of their heritage for their children in order to pass it on from one generation to another. They have no idea from where they are going to get the money. If this government is really serious about multiculturalism in this country, that money would be reinstated.
We Canadians are very fortunate to live in this cultural mosaic that is called Canada. As I mentioned earlier, many of us are Canadian born, but there is equally a great number who come from other lands from around the world who have chosen Canada as their country.
We must not be smug or casual about our way of life. We see great division in this country today, a division that is extremely distressing for people of all cultures. I would just like to mention one. This morning my colleague stood up in the House of Commons under Standing Order 31 and mentioned the desecration of a cemetery, anti-Semitic actions against a Jewish cemetery in France. We cannot tolerate this kind of action.
Our Sikh community has been discriminated against probably more in some parts of the country than in others. There have been great discussions with regard to allowing turbans in the RCMP.
Our native peoples have been discriminated against for years. They were the original Canadians. Yet they probably have been the most discriminated against group of people that this country has ever seen.
Again, I have been very pleased to stand here and speak on this bill this afternoon, a bill that we have to support. Although it is weak and although it does not provide enough, if Canada is to move ahead and recognize the cultural mosaic that we are, then we must have an act to establish a Department of Multiculturalism and Citizenship.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it gives me a great deal of pleasure to talk to a principle and a philosophy that we desperately need for the Canadian experiment to become a reality in our country. Although founded by the aboriginal peoples of our land, the reality of Canada emerged with the arrival of the English and the French. We have added to the stream which is Canada with that third more important and growing sector, the multicultural dimension.
That reality was recognized in the early seventies when the principle and philosophy of multiculturalism was brought forward in the framework of a bilingualism policy by my predecessor for Mount Royal, former Prime Minister Trudeau, in October of 1971. It was at that time of the B and B commission that some serious observations were made about this third strand in our society, the multicultural community. Although we all knew that that sector was there and was enriching us all, we did not quite identify the kind of measures that were needed to make sure that this new kind of Canada would grow in tolerance, understanding, appreciation and respect for the differences.
We were, in this experiment, very different from the American experience. One did not come here, like one would come into the United States, and immediately salute the flag and forget one's roots. That is one way to proceed. In Canada, people were invited to bring their culture and their heritage. They were told to respect their roots, honour their ancestors and add to the Canadian experience, never denying who or what they were.
I think that is a very exciting dimension, but it has problems inherent in it. When one comes from lands of intolerance or lands that promote discrimination or fight over language, race, creed or culture, there is obviously the tendency to bring along those inherent structures and that frame of mind which has developed through history and through geography.
We say to those people: "You have now moved to a country that has a new concept. Be part of the mainstream; be proud as a Canadian". We say to you, through public institutions, whether it is through our broadcast-
Govemment Orders
ing services, radio or television, whether it is through the printed media, whether through magazines, books, or any other ways in which we express ourselves in a cultural sense in this country, "We admire who you are; we want to know more about what you are".
Madam Speaker, those are perhaps idealistic ways and, perhaps, some people would say, a very Pollyanna view of how Canada is to grow and flourish. I do not believe that that is being Pollyanna. I think it is perhaps somewhat visionary. It could be realized if a truly multicultural bill were put into this House, as a bridging mechanism for all Canadians and not directed strictly to visible minorities, not directed strictly to our aboriginal founding peoples, not directed to minorities per se, but directed to all Canadians in an inter-active way, so that we can learn to appreciate, respect and even love each other.
My colleague from the Ottawa region alluded to a comment I made earlier today with respect to desecration of sacred land, of consecrated ground, cemeteries. I cannot think of any more mischievous, nefarious, and hurtful way to attack a community than to attack a place where families go to pay respect to ancestors who have given of themselves and passed on.
That is not the Canadian way; that is not the tolerant way; and that is not indicative of the love and affection we share for each other regardless of race, religion, language, creed, or country of origin. These are acts of racism we have seen manifest against our aboriginal peoples, as we have seen in the Donald Marshall and other cases with respect to our Indian population, as we have recently seen through Disparaitre on Radio Canada.
This was an insensitive documentary, very one-sided, presented by a woman, also very narrow-minded, who was named to head the fiftieth anniversary celebrations in Quebec, which was to celebrate all women and all women's contributions in Quebec. However they forgot to include visible minorities in their planning, forgot to include English-speaking women in much of their planning. They went ahead, 3,500 of them, and raised their glasses in a toast to the wonders of Quebec and Quebec women. Yes, I can tell you that we can toast the wonders of Quebec and Quebec women. But forget the narrowminded people who have forgotten to open their minds. That is why we need a bill like this.

Government Orders
I can tell you about Madeleine Parent. She is a wonderful women 71 years of age, with a long line of history and family in Quebec, a trade unionist who fought against racism, fought for the under-privileged, fought for employment equity, and fought for the right of all women to have their place equally in this society. It didn't matter their colour, but it was important that a voice spoke out.
I can tell you about women from the Indian community who fought for the rights of the Indian woman to be recognized as a person with fair and equal rights with her brothers in this society.
There are many areas that need to be approached. The problem with this bill is really an unfortunate one and makes me question the government's thinking. Unfortunately, the whole question of the definition of multicul-turalism is unclear. That is regrettable. Perhaps it will evolve in time and amendments will be adopted, because they are desperately needed. From strong support from the Canadian Ethnocultural Council in 1987, 1988, and 1989, we now have serious reservations from them on May 11, 1990, as they see the cynicism behind this bill, the lack of sincerity because of its weakness.
They are very unhappy about the definition of multi-culturalism. They are very unhappy that the bill does not link itself to the Canadian Multiculturalism Act. They are unhappy with these weaselly words "should", "perhaps", "may", "shall", nothing that is directive or concrete.
There is nothing that will ensure employment equity. That bill, too, which is coming up again, is a sham.
The bill is weak, but the principle and the philosophy is important. As the term does not include "multiracial" I was wondering if the multiracials are included? As it does not include the aboriginals, are they included in this mandate? Is this to promote integration of men, women, and children, and if so, how? What are the educational parameters? What is the relationship with our provinces? Is it at the First Ministers' table? What kinds of directives and powers are given to this minister and his ministry, because it is important, if we believe in a vision of Canada, for all people to understand. Is its purpose to ensure a sensitivity and an upgrading on the employment equity act? Will there to be grants and support to cultural groups, or is it another song and dance, an
opportunity for all of us, including myself who might take advantage of it, to go and hand out a grant?
That is not its purpose. It is too important. We should have laid out ministerial responsibilities. We should have ensured that projects like the heritage language project, aboriginals communication, which is not only for aboriginals, but for the whole north, should never have been cut.
There are so many serious funding questions to be asked. Since it is important to move ahead with this bill, I flag them as questions, not as a destruction of the concept. It is a pretty package. The question is over its content.
What about staffing? All members of this House know that if you do not put sufficient funding into a project, you do not end up with a proper goal. We cannot realistically expect projects of principles and philosophy to grow if they do not have staff and management and some funds behind it.
I want to know how this will be put it into effect so that we get knowledgeable representative people who reflect the whole society, men and women of all races, colours and creeds, who can work together to implement a wonderful philosophy that is the Canada of tomorrow. It will be a unique nation among nations if we can meet the goal.
Supporting this policy would be a joy. I support it, but it is not the joy I would have liked, because the objectives are not as focused as I think they should be. The issues, policies and programs are not sufficiently clear to address what is fundamentally a very vital issue as we depend more and more on immigration. We have to make sure that everyone, even if they have been here for hundreds of years, learns to live, respect, grow and glorify in our own differences. Otherwise, the will is puffy and pretentious and does not do what it was meant to do. I think that would be an unconscionable message and not one that I think the present minister of state would want to leave. That is not the nature of this man. I believe he is a person of goodwill but I think he is being frustrated at the ministerial table. That is most regrettable.
I have said most of the things that have been in my heart with respect to this bill. I thank you very much for the patience to listen.
May 11, 1990

In my riding I am seeing increased intolerance between racial groups who have come from many parts of this world; from Asia, Africa, the Caribbean, the Middle East, the Far East, from all parts of the globe. They are not getting alone right now, either as newly arrived or as the indigenous population.
This ministry, and this minister, have an incredible challenge for all of us. Together we must ensure that he has the funds, staff, and mandate to see that something concrete and helpful takes place in this country.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, of all the times I have risen in the House as a member of the opposition, never before have I wished so dearly that I would not have to be standing here in opposition.
In the matters of multiculturalism and citizenship, I would have hoped that the development of this department was an attempt by the government to take us to the next step of helping us to define what Canada is. It would have been a wonderful thing to stand here and speak without having to make any kind of criticism-opposition, possibly, but in the sense of being able to make what are sometimes called friendly amendments to the proposition before us. Unfortunately, that is not the case and, in spite of the fact that it is not, I am not going to go criticize too much criticism, because that has been well done by other speakers.
I know time is limited and I would like to dwell on some other things with respect to this department in this context.
In this context, let me start this way. I am white, that is rather obvious. If you were to look at the spelling of my name, Madam Speaker, you would probably conclude, and rightly so, that I am an Anglo-Saxon. You could draw some conclusions from that as well. I willingly add that I am also Protestant which makes me a WASP.
In the context of what is going on in our country today, I certainly speak for the members of my Party who say it is inexcusable that organizations in this country are trying so hard to steer their communities towards an English-only approach. I say that as a WASP who cannot accept that. I would also say, being a monolingual White Anglo-Saxon Protestant, in the context of this very thing in Canada today and having had to look at myself within that context, that I would suggest that a lot of the
problems from these groups stem from a feeling of arrogance.
As a White Anglo-Saxon Protestant, I do not have to learn another language. Almost all those who have ever come to our country have accommodated to what is essentially my culture. I think that is a tremendously large part of the problem we are facing today. It is unfortunate, and I would say to those who are of British origin: "Smarten up! There is no particular reason why you should feel arrogant. There may be some reasons for you to feel culturally disadvantaged, but there are ways to overcome that as well."
I would hope that there are few in the House and in the nation who do not feel joy, if you will, at the skirl of a Scottish bagpipe, and when you add the drums, you have an added pleasure. Is there anyone in this nation who has not heard a Welsh choir? That is certainly part of my culture. Is there anyone in this nation, particularly those watching who are here today, who would deny the English the tradition of what we are doing at this moment, and what I am doing at this moment?
I would say to those of English origin: "Get involved within your own cultural milieu in your communities. Envelope that which is British and develop a greater appreciation for the other cultures within your community as well."
I know that co-operation among linguistic, ethnic or cultural groups cannot be fostered by law. As a matter of fact, when people are forced into that kind of co-operation, it has the opposite effect and animosities are thereby engendered. As law-makers, it is possible to assist the co-operation which we are aiming toward and of which we are part.
This is the third reading of the bill which establishes the Department of Multiculturalism and Citizenship. A great opportunity has been lost because the government was not willing to envelope some of the suggestions made by the opposition parties. Those suggestions would have gone so much farther toward aiding the evolution of a nation of which we all so proud and of which multiculturalism forms such a great part. The problem is that that did not take place. Now, all we can express is a feeling and a prescience of what we would hope would
May 11, 1990

either be amendments to this or the next succession to this concept within our nation.
One of the surprises I had as a Member of Parliament was being introduced to Citizenship Court. That prompts me to suggest that the name of the department is reversed. It would have been so much better had it been the department of citizenship and multiculturalism. That is not the case, but a good case can be made for that being what should have occurred.
As a member of Parliament, one of the greatest pleasures I have is going to Citizenship Court. There are three or four different reasons why I find it so pleasurable. The first one reminds me that it was not always possible to be a Canadian citizen. When I was younger, there was no such thing as Canadian citizenship. When I went across the country and entered a different school, the first thing the teacher asked was: "What is your national origin?" Of course, my answer was: "Scots." That is why I referred to the bagpipe first in my references to the wonderful things which have come out of the British Isles in the cultural sense.

speechtext:
that Bill S-15, an Act to amend the Act of incorporation of Desjardins Mutual Life Assurance Company, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to give you details about the Act to amend the Act of incorporation of Desjardins Mutual Life Assurance Company, and act to permit Desjardins Mutual Life Assurance Company, a federally incorporated company, to be continued as a corporation under the laws of the Province of Quebec.
Bill S-15 is similar to Bill S-5 passed by the Senate on June 29, 1989 to authorize The Safeguard Life Assurance Company, the other life assurance company of the Desjardins Movement, to come under Quebec jurisdiction.
All the organizations or body corporates of the Desjardins Movement operate under Quebec laws, except the Desjardins Mutual Life Assurance Company and its
recently acquired subsidiary, Laurier Life Holding Limited which controls Laurier Life Insurance.
Desjardins Mutual Life Assurance Company does most of its business in Quebec. The Desjardins Movement wants to merge Desjardins Mutual Life Assurance Company with La Sauvegarde in order to consolidate its operations in Quebec and thus benefit from potential synergy within the Movement. This initiative was taken in the over-all context of the restructuration of the Desjardins Movement initiated last year.
A change in jurisdiction is necessary since the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act, which Desjardins Mutual Life Assurance Company now comes under, does not allow mergers with a company under provincial jurisdiction. This change also follows a decision taken at the March 21, 1990 special meeting of the Company's members that was convened specifically to authorize the continuance of Desjardins Mutual Life Assurance Company under Quebec legislation and to introduce a private bill to that effect in the Canadian Parliament.
All members of Desjardins Mutual Life Assurance Company, in other words, all policy holders, were mailed an invitation to this meeting, with a proxy form enabling them to vote. The vast majority of them voted in favour ot the proposal.
The company that will emerge from the merger of Desjardins Mutual Life Assurance Company with La Sauvegarde will become number one in Quebec in the insurance sector.
The government's policy for charter repatriation is to grant such requests from mutual insurance companies unless the policyholders object, which is not the case for Desjardins Mutual Life Assurance. Furthermore, the federal government recognizes that a financial institution's decision to come under one jurisdiction or another at a particular time depends on the amount and kind of business it does and on its plans for expansion.
The federal government wishes to accommodate the desires of financial institutions in this regard. To this end, I move that the House pass this bill and I believe that hon. members would agree to refer it to the finance committee instead of the legislative committee as mentioned in the introduction.

I thank everyone for their co-operation in this matter.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I am proud to support the motion of the hon. member for Levis (Mr. Fontaine) concerning this Life Assurance Company. We, in the opposition, also agree to his suggestion that this bill be referred to the Standing Committee on Finance instead of a legislative committee. Since the bill will be studied in the finance committee where we will have the opportunity to put forward some ideas and suggestions, I will not pursue the matter any further this afternoon.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PRIVATE BILLS   ACT OF INCORPORATION OF DESJARDINS MUTUAL LIFE ASSURANCE COMPANY MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I also wish to inform the House that the New Democratic Party supports the bill at second reading and is quite happy to have it referred to the Standing Committee on Finance.
We note that this is the second time this year that the Desjardins group has had to come to this House to ask for special legislation to regroup itself under Quebec law. We are wondering if this is not because of the delay of the federal government in bringing forward a new
Private Members' Business
framework for financial institutions and we are thinking that maybe the other approach is better. Therefore, we are hoping that the finance committee will take this opportunity to look at these factors also.
